scenes.tts: How does a cell spot a microbe it has never met, and switch on defense genes within minutes? Antibodies take days to arrive. Yet a macrophage starts changing its genes right away.
scenes.caption: How does a cell spot a microbe it has never met, and switch on defense genes within minutes? Antibodies take days to arrive. Yet a macrophage starts changing its genes right away.
scenes.visual: 16:9 dark canvas filling at least 60% of frame height with a macrophage cross-section: plasma membrane arch across the top, an endosome bubble on the left, cytosol across the center, and a purple nucleus at the bottom. An amber bacterium drifts toward the top membrane while a sleek timer dial ticks gently in minutes. Labels: 'Macrophage', 'Nucleus', 'Minutes'.
scenes.narration: How does a cell spot a microbe it has never met, and switch on defense genes within minutes? Antibodies take days to arrive. Yet a macrophage starts changing its genes right away.

scenes.visual: The macrophage cross-section softens slightly as the title 'An Alarm Held Ready' glides in at top center in crisp white text, then fades out cleanly while the amber bacterium keeps drifting.

scenes.tts: The cell uses a short list of Toll-like receptors. Each receptor recognizes a shared microbial molecule that microbes cannot give up. Receptors for outer coats sit on the cell surface. Receptors for microbial nucleic acids wait inside endosomes, the bubbles where swallowed microbes break open.
scenes.caption: The cell uses a short list of Toll-like receptors. Each receptor recognizes a shared microbial molecule that microbes cannot give up. scenes.visual: Colour map established: amber for microbial patterns, teal for Toll-like receptors and their kinase relay, sky blue for lysine-63 scaffold chains, coral for inhibitors and destruction tags, emerald for NF-κB, purple for nucleus and DNA. On the top membrane, teal horseshoe receptors meet amber bacterial coat fragments. Inside the left endosome bubble, an amber microbe breaks open, releasing strands that meet inward-facing teal horseshoes. Labels: 'Surface: outer coats', 'Endosome: nucleic acids'.

scenes.tts: The gene switch, NF kappa B, is already built and folded before any microbe arrives. A coral inhibitor called I kappa B wraps around it and covers its nuclear entry tag. While that inhibitor holds tight, the switch stays trapped outside.
scenes.caption: The gene switch, NF-κB, is already built and folded before any microbe arrives. A coral inhibitor called IκB wraps around it and covers its nuclear entry tag. While that inhibitor holds tight, the switch stays trapped outside.
scenes.visual: Camera glides into the cytosol of the same macrophage. An emerald paired block labelled 'NF-κB' gently bobs inside a curved coral clamp labelled 'IκB' that covers a glowing purple key-tab labelled 'Nuclear tag'. Soft dashed arrows trying to pull emerald NF-κB toward the purple nucleus bounce off the coral clamp.
scenes.narration: The gene switch, NF-κB, is already built and folded before any microbe arrives. A coral inhibitor called IκB wraps around it and covers its nuclear entry tag. While that inhibitor holds tight, the switch stays trapped outside.

scenes.tts: How does a touch outside break that clamp? When bacterial endotoxin binds the receptor TLR4 with its partner MD 2, two teal receptors move side by side. Their inner tails pair and dock an adaptor, MyD88. MyD88 stacks with IRAK kinases into a helical tower so they activate one another.
scenes.caption: How does a touch outside break that clamp? When bacterial endotoxin binds the receptor TLR4 with its partner MD-2, two teal receptors move side by side. Their inner tails pair and dock an adaptor, MyD88. MyD88 stacks with IRAK kinases into a helical tower so they activate one another.
scenes.visual: At the top membrane, an amber endotoxin block bridges two teal TLR4/MD-2 horseshoes, sliding them side by side. Their inner teal tails touch, and teal adaptor blocks ('MyD88') dock below. Teal IRAK kinase blocks spiral smoothly into a stacked helical tower beneath them; bright pulses ripple between neighboring IRAK blocks to show activation. Label: 'MyD88–IRAK tower (schematic)'.
scenes.narration: How does a touch outside break that clamp? When bacterial endotoxin binds the receptor TLR4 with its partner MD-2, two teal receptors move side by side. Their inner tails pair and dock an adaptor, MyD88. MyD88 stacks with IRAK kinases into a helical tower so they activate one another.

scenes.tts: Next comes a surprise about ubiquitin. An activated IRAK engages TRAF6, which builds a sky-blue ubiquitin chain linked through lysine 63. This chain destroys nothing. Instead, it acts as a scaffold gathering two kinases, TAK1 and IKK, side by side. Right on that platform, TAK1 switches IKK on.
scenes.caption: Next comes a surprise about ubiquitin. An activated IRAK engages TRAF6, which builds a sky-blue ubiquitin chain linked through lysine-63. This chain destroys nothing. Instead, it acts as a scaffold gathering two kinases, TAK1 and IKK, side by side. Right on that platform, TAK1 switches IKK on.
scenes.visual: Below the teal tower, a teal block ('TRAF6') spins out a growing sky-blue chain of linked beads labelled 'K63 scaffold'. Two teal kinase complexes ('TAK1' and 'IKK') glide in and dock side by side on the sky-blue chain. A bright activation spark arcs from TAK1 onto IKK, lighting IKK up.
scenes.narration: Next comes a surprise about ubiquitin. An activated IRAK engages TRAF6, which builds a sky-blue ubiquitin chain linked through lysine-63. This chain destroys nothing. Instead, it acts as a scaffold gathering two kinases, TAK1 and IKK, side by side. Right on that platform, TAK1 switches IKK on.

scenes.tts: Active IKK moves to the coral clamp and stamps two phosphate marks onto I kappa B. Even then, the clamp hangs on. Those marks summon a second enzyme that attaches a coral lysine 48 ubiquitin chain. That tag sends the inhibitor to the proteasome, the cell's protein shredder, which frees emerald NF kappa B.
scenes.caption: Active IKK moves to the coral clamp and stamps two phosphate marks onto IκB. Even then, the clamp hangs on. Those marks summon a second enzyme that attaches a coral lysine-48 ubiquitin chain. That tag sends the inhibitor to the proteasome, the cell's protein shredder, which frees emerald NF-κB.
scenes.visual: Lit teal IKK glides to the coral IκB clamp and stamps two bright dots onto it. The clamp stays shut until a second enzyme attaches a coral chain labelled 'K48 tag'. A dark barrel ('Proteasome') draws the coral IκB clamp away and shreds it into fading coral fragments, unveiling the glowing purple nuclear tag on emerald NF-κB.
scenes.narration: Active IKK moves to the coral clamp and stamps two phosphate marks onto IκB. Even then, the clamp hangs on. Those marks summon a second enzyme that attaches a coral lysine-48 ubiquitin chain. That tag sends the inhibitor to the proteasome, the cell's protein shredder, which frees emerald NF-κB.

scenes.tts: Now pause and predict. Suppose a mutant NF kappa B lacks its nuclear entry tag. Endotoxin arrives, and I kappa B is destroyed as usual. Will the defense genes switch on? Take a few seconds to decide.
scenes.caption: Now pause and predict. Suppose a mutant NF-κB lacks its nuclear entry tag. Endotoxin arrives, and IκB is destroyed as usual. Will the defense genes switch on? Take a few seconds to decide.
scenes.visual: In the same macrophage frame, a mutant emerald NF-κB block sits free of its coral clamp, but its purple nuclear tag is drawn as an empty outline with a cross. A question card overlays the upper cytosol: 'No nuclear tag: do defense genes switch on?' Amber endotoxin rests on the top teal receptors as the question settles.
scenes.narration: Now pause and predict. Suppose a mutant NF-κB lacks its nuclear entry tag. Endotoxin arrives, and IκB is destroyed as usual. Will the defense genes switch on? Take a few seconds to decide.

scenes.visual: Thinking pause: the question 'No nuclear tag: do defense genes switch on?' remains clearly on screen while a subtle progress bar fills slowly along the bottom of the card over 4.5 seconds and the macrophage background breathes softly.

scenes.tts: No, they stay off, because destroying the clamp helps only by uncovering that tag. The tag is what carries the switch through the nuclear pores. In a normal cell, freed emerald NF kappa B glides into the purple nucleus and binds target DNA. Nothing new must be made, so defense genes switch on within minutes.
scenes.caption: No, they stay off, because destroying the clamp helps only by uncovering that tag. The tag is what carries the switch through the nuclear pores. In a normal cell, freed emerald NF-κB glides into the purple nucleus and binds target DNA. Nothing new must be made, so defense genes switch on within minutes.
scenes.visual: The question card clears to a coral mark 'No: genes stay off', and the tagless mutant NF-κB bounces off a nuclear pore. Beside it, a normal emerald NF-κB with its glowing purple tag glides through the pore into the purple nucleus, wraps around a stylized purple DNA bar, and waves of light pulse outward from the gene. Label: 'Normal cell: defense genes ON within minutes'.
scenes.narration: No, they stay off, because destroying the clamp helps only by uncovering that tag. The tag is what carries the switch through the nuclear pores. scenes.tts: This rule covers canonical Toll-like receptor signaling to NF kappa B. A few routes, such as TLR3, instead steer mainly toward interferon. In the core pathway, the activator waits built and trapped. When a microbial pattern arrives, the relay triggers inhibitor destruction for an answer within minutes.

scenes.visual: Wide view of the macrophage cross-section showing the full glowing path from amber pattern at teal receptors, down the sky-blue K63 scaffold, past shredded coral IκB, to emerald NF-κB on purple DNA. A small muted side branch from the endosome briefly reads 'TLR3 → interferon'. The frame fades smoothly to dark.

scenes.visual: Clean dark end card displaying one centered line only, with no smaller line underneath: 'Toll-like receptors free pre-made NF-κB by triggering inhibitor destruction.'
